add(no="1", title="90-Day Award Deadline Running from Constitution of the Tribunal", sev="Critical",
clause="\"The arbitrator shall render a final award within 90 calendar days of the constitution of the tribunal.\" (MSA s. 14.2)",
rules="Art. 24.1 (best-efforts target of 180 calendar days, running from the last substantive hearing or last authorised written submission, whichever is later); Art. 24.2 (SAI Court may extend); Art. 24.3 (time limit is a target; late award not invalid); Art. 24.4 (period runs from last hearing/submission, not from constitution); Art. 8.1 (constitution occurs on confirmation/appointment plus filed declarations); Art. 9.2 and 13.2 (provisional timetable and case management conference within 21 days of receipt of the file); Art. 25.5 (award notified only once costs paid); Art. 1.4 (party agreement prevails unless it contravenes a mandatory Rule, the law of the seat, or the SAI Court finds it renders the arbitration impracticable).",
analysis=[
"Nature of the deviation. The clause departs from Article 24 on three axes at once: (i) length (90 days versus 180 days); (ii) trigger (constitution of the tribunal versus the close of the evidentiary phase; Article 24.4 expressly excludes the constitution-to-merits period that the clause makes the whole of the window); and (iii) character (the clause is framed as a mandatory obligation (\"shall render\") whereas Article 24 is a best-efforts target whose breach expressly does not invalidate the award (Art. 24.3)). In practical terms the clause allows roughly one-sixth to one-tenth of the time the Rules contemplate for an entire proceeding.",
"Feasibility. Within the 90 days the tribunal must: receive the file and fix a provisional timetable (up to 21 days, Art. 9.2); hold the case management conference (Art. 13.2); receive at least one round of written submissions from each side (Art. 14.1) on an $11.9 million claim and a $1.4 million counterclaim; manage document production on technical server and API data; receive witness statements and forensic expert reports (Palladian on our side, presumably a Kuiper expert in reply); manage a bilingual English/German record (Issue 6); hold any hearing a party requests (Art. 16.1); deliberate; and draft a reasoned award (Art. 25.2) that also fixes costs (Art. 25.4). This is not realistically achievable in a contested, expert-driven, bilingual case of this value.",
"Which prevails. Under Article 1.4 the parties' agreement prevails over Article 24. Article 24 is not identified as mandatory, the Rules nowhere designate which provisions are \"mandatory\", and a short time limit does not on its face contravene Singapore law. The 90-day limit therefore likely binds the tribunal as a limit on its mandate. The SAI Court could invoke Article 1.4(c) (impracticability), but an institutional decision to disregard the parties' express time limit would itself create a ground for challenge (see below). It is also doubtful that the SAI Court's power to extend under Article 24.2 reaches a contractual (as opposed to Rules-based) deadline, and the savings language in Article 24.3 is expressed to apply to \"the time limit under Article 24.1\", not to a limit agreed by the parties.",
"Enforceability risk (seat law: Singapore). The International Arbitration Act 1994 (\"IAA\") gives the UNCITRAL Model Law force of law. An award rendered after the agreed deadline is exposed to set-aside under Model Law Art. 34(2)(a)(iv) (arbitral procedure not in accordance with the parties' agreement) and potentially Art. 34(2)(a)(iii) (tribunal acting after its mandate expired), and to refusal of recognition abroad under New York Convention Art. V(1)(d). Unlike the domestic Arbitration Act 2001 (s. 36, court power to extend time for making an award), the IAA does not, to our understanding, contain an express equivalent court power to extend a contractually agreed award deadline; this must be confirmed with Singapore counsel. Conversely, an award rushed out within 90 days on a truncated record invites a due-process challenge under Model Law Art. 18 / Art. 34(2)(a)(ii) and IAA s. 24(b) (breach of natural justice) if either side is denied a reasonable opportunity to present its case (cf. SAI Art. 18.1).",
"Strategic implications for Greenleaf. As claimant, Greenleaf carries the burden of proof (Art. 14.2) on technically complex causation (server-side corruption versus Greenleaf API configuration) and quantum. A compressed timetable disproportionately harms the party with the burden. It also hands Kuiper a tactical option: participate slowly, allow day 90 to pass, and then attack any adverse award as out of time. Qualified candidates (who also need cloud/data and life-sciences expertise and, per Issue 6, ideally German) may decline appointment because the deadline is unrealistic and exposes them to an ultra vires award.",
"Applicable-law note. The deadline is a procedural matter governed by the seat (MSA s. 14.1(b) expressly allocates procedural law to the seat). New York substantive law does not cure or aggravate the problem, although the arbitration agreement itself may be governed by New York law (see Issue 13), under which agreed time limits in arbitration agreements are also generally enforced."],
kuiper="Kuiper's October 28, 2024 email does not address the 90-day deadline. Its stated insistence on full German-language submissions and a 30-day (rather than 15-day) appointment window would further compress the effective time available.",
recs=[
"Make this the centrepiece of a pre-filing procedural agreement with Kuiper (see Part F). Propose a written amendment under Article 1.2 replacing the 90-day limit with the Article 24 regime (or, at minimum, a deadline running from the close of proceedings, with an express power of the SAI Court to extend). Kuiper has an equal interest in an enforceable award on its $1.4 million counterclaim, and its own email emphasises an \"orderly and efficient\" process.",
"If no amendment is agreed before filing, raise the issue in the Request (Art. 4.2(e) observations) and ask the tribunal at the first case management conference to record in Terms of Reference (Art. 13.1) signed by both parties an agreed extension. Any party agreement must be express and in writing; do not rely on implied waiver under Art. 30 alone.",
"Do not invite the SAI Court to override the clause unilaterally under Art. 1.4(c) without Kuiper's agreement, because that would itself create a Model Law Art. 34(2)(a)(iv) argument.",
"Brief prospective arbitrators on the deadline issue during candidate screening so that any appointment is made with eyes open; prefer candidates willing to proceed on the basis of a written party agreement to extend.",
"Instruct Singapore counsel to confirm (i) whether the Singapore High Court has power under the IAA to extend an agreed award deadline, and (ii) how Singapore courts treat late awards under an agreed time limit."])

add(no="2", title="Exclusion of Punitive, Exemplary and Consequential Damages; Conflict with MSA Section 12.2", sev="Critical",
clause="\"The arbitrator shall not have the authority to award punitive, exemplary, or consequential damages.\" (MSA s. 14.2). Compare MSA s. 12.2 (exclusion of indirect, incidental, special and consequential damages, EXCEPT for Section 13 indemnification obligations and willful misconduct or fraud, and listing loss of revenue, profits, business, loss of data (other than the restoration obligation under Section 7.4) and cost of substitute services as excluded categories); MSA s. 12.1 ($15 million aggregate cap, subject to the same carve-outs).",
rules="Art. 34.1(a) (tribunal may award damages \"whether compensatory, consequential, or otherwise available under the applicable law\"); Art. 34.2 (no punitive or exemplary damages unless authorised by the applicable substantive law); Art. 34.3 (parties may agree to limit remedies; such agreement \"shall be given effect\" subject to mandatory applicable law); Art. 11.1 and 23.1 (tribunal applies the parties' chosen substantive law, here New York law).",
analysis=[
"Deviation from the Rules. The clause narrows the default remedial power in Art. 34.1(a), which expressly includes consequential damages. Article 34.3 authorises exactly this kind of limitation, so the clause is a permitted modification rather than a conflict with a mandatory Rule. On punitive and exemplary damages the clause is broadly consistent with Art. 34.2 and with New York law, which does not permit punitive damages for ordinary breach of contract absent conduct directed at the public (Rocanova v. Equitable Life Assurance Society, 83 N.Y.2d 603 (1994)) and historically treats arbitral awards of punitive damages as contrary to public policy (Garrity v. Lyle Stuart, Inc., 40 N.Y.2d 354 (1976); but see Mastrobuono v. Shearson Lehman Hutton, Inc., 514 U.S. 52 (1995) on the FAA). The punitive/exemplary limb therefore costs Greenleaf little.",
"Internal conflict within the MSA (most significant point). Section 12.2 excludes consequential damages but expressly preserves them for (i) Section 13 indemnification obligations and (ii) willful misconduct or fraud. Section 14.2 contains no such carve-outs: it strips the arbitrator of authority to award consequential damages at all. Because the arbitration is the exclusive forum (s. 14.2: \"resolved exclusively by binding arbitration\"), the practical effect of s. 14.2 read literally is to eliminate the s. 12.2 carve-outs, including the willful misconduct/fraud carve-out that may be Greenleaf's best route to the $3.2 million. Arguments for Greenleaf: (a) the specific, negotiated risk-allocation provision (s. 12, described in s. 12.3 as \"an essential basis of the bargain\") should control over a general sentence in a procedural clause; (b) contracts are read as a whole to give effect to every provision, and reading s. 14.2 literally would render the s. 12.2 carve-outs meaningless in the only available forum; (c) any ambiguity is construed against the drafter, and the arbitration clause was proposed by Kuiper's counsel (Feldhammer Grau) and accepted with minimal revision (contra proferentem is a weak, last-resort canon between sophisticated, represented parties, but it is available). Kuiper will argue that s. 14.2 is a later-in-sequence, specific limitation on the tribunal's authority. This is an open construction question that a tribunal will decide under New York law.",
"Seat-law overlay (Singapore). Because s. 14.2 is framed as a limit on the arbitrator's \"authority\", an award of consequential damages could be attacked at the seat as exceeding the scope of the submission to arbitration (Model Law Art. 34(2)(a)(iii)) and resisted abroad under New York Convention Art. V(1)(c). Singapore courts do not review the merits, so a tribunal's reasoned construction of ss. 12.2/14.2 is unlikely to be disturbed, but the framing increases challenge risk if the tribunal awards consequential losses. The question of whether the exclusion is enforceable at all is one of New York substantive law (s. 14.1; Art. 23.1); the question of whether the tribunal stayed within its mandate is a seat-law question. This is the clearest instance of the New York / Singapore bifurcation the assignment asks us to examine.",
"Enforceability under New York law. New York enforces consequential-damages exclusions negotiated between sophisticated commercial parties. However, New York public policy will not enforce an exculpatory clause to shield a party from liability for gross negligence or intentional wrongdoing (Kalisch-Jarcho, Inc. v. City of New York, 58 N.Y.2d 377 (1983); Sommer v. Federal Signal Corp., 79 N.Y.2d 540 (1992)). If the forensic evidence supports gross negligence or willful misconduct (for example, knowing failure to remediate a known defect, or deletion of server logs after the September 12 notice), Greenleaf can argue the exclusion in s. 14.2 is unenforceable to that extent as a matter of New York public policy, which reinforces the s. 12.2 carve-out argument.",
"Recharacterisation of the $3.2 million outage losses. Under New York law, the line is between general (direct) damages, which are the natural and probable consequence of the breach, and consequential damages, which arise from collateral transactions or special circumstances (Kenford Co. v. County of Erie, 73 N.Y.2d 312 (1989)). In Biotronik A.G. v. Conor Medsystems Ireland, Ltd., 22 N.Y.3d 799 (2014), the Court of Appeals held that lost profits can be general damages where they are the direct and probable result of the breach and flow from the very bargain itself. Arguments: (a) uninterrupted availability of the LIMS platform was the core performance obligation, so the cost of 47 days of non-availability (lost productivity of laboratory staff, workarounds) is the direct value of the lost performance; (b) costs incurred to mitigate the outages (manual processing, temporary substitute tools) are recoverable mitigation costs rather than consequential losses; (c) a reduction in or refund of fees for the period of non-performance is direct damage. Weaker components: third-party vendor penalties and \"delayed commercial milestones\" depend on collateral contracts and are most exposed to being classed as consequential. Note that s. 12.2 expressly lists \"cost of procurement of substitute services\" and \"loss of business\" as excluded categories, which undercuts certain mitigation and milestone arguments.",
"Exposure of the $8.7 million \"direct\" claim. This risk is not identified in the assignment memorandum. Section 12.2 lists \"loss of data (other than the Service Provider's obligation to restore data under Section 7.4)\" among the excluded categories of indirect damages. Kuiper will argue that much of the $8.7 million (in particular delayed trial timelines and FDA re-submission costs) is consequential loss of data, and that only Section 7.4 restoration is recoverable. Greenleaf's strongest position is to anchor the data-reconstruction costs to Kuiper's Section 7.4 restoration obligation (which is excepted from the exclusion) and to characterise re-submission costs as the direct cost of restoring compliant data. We have not been provided with Section 7.4 or Section 13; both must be reviewed before the Request is drafted.",
"Internal characterisation risk. The assignment memorandum itself labels the $3.2 million as \"consequential\". That label is privileged work product, but Greenleaf's pleadings, correspondence (including the September 12 notice), expert reports and internal board materials should not adopt it. The Request should plead the outage losses as direct/general damages."],
kuiper="Not addressed in the October 28 email, but Kuiper's denial of breach and attribution to Greenleaf's API configuration indicates it will contest causation and quantum vigorously; the exclusion gives it a second line of defence.",
recs=[
"Obtain and review MSA Sections 7.4 (data restoration) and 13 (indemnification) immediately, together with the September 12, 2024 notice of breach, to check how the claims were characterised.",
"Re-model the $11.9 million claim into (a) direct performance/restoration damages anchored to Section 7.4, (b) mitigation costs, and (c) residual items at risk of exclusion; quantify the downside if (c) is excluded.",
"Plead, in the alternative, (i) that the s. 12.2 carve-outs for willful misconduct and fraud apply notwithstanding s. 14.2, and (ii) that New York public policy (Kalisch-Jarcho) bars enforcement of the exclusion against grossly negligent or intentional conduct. Direct Palladian to look specifically for evidence bearing on gross negligence or willful conduct, including any post-notice log deletion.",
"Consider whether any element of the claim falls within the Section 13 indemnity (for example, third-party vendor penalties), which is carved out of both the cap and the s. 12.2 exclusion.",
"Avoid the word \"consequential\" in all external documents; instruct the client accordingly."])

add(no="3", title="Emergency Arbitrator and Interim Relief for Preservation of Server Logs", sev="Critical",
clause="Section 14.2 is silent on emergency arbitrator relief and contains no opt-out. Section 14.3(d): nothing in the escalation procedure \"shall prevent a Party from seeking emergency or interim relief pursuant to the arbitration rules referenced in Section 14.2 or from a court of competent jurisdiction where such relief is necessary to prevent irreparable harm.\"",
rules="Art. 15.1(a) (tribunal may order preservation of evidence); Art. 15.4 (recourse to courts for interim measures not a waiver); Art. 15.5 and Art. 15bis (emergency arbitrator before constitution); Art. 15bis.2 / EA-3 (appointment within 2 business days of application and fee); Art. 15bis.4 (applies unless (a) parties opted out or (b) the arbitration agreement was concluded before the effective date of the edition first introducing the procedure); EA-1 (application contents, including irreparable harm); EA-2 (CHF 20,000 non-refundable fee); EA-4 (schedule within 2 business days of appointment); EA-5 (decision within 15 calendar days, binding, may be order or award); EA-6 (costs); EA-7 (applies unless the parties \"expressly opted out in their arbitration agreement\").",
analysis=[
"Availability confirmed, with one verification point. The emergency arbitrator procedure is available to Greenleaf. (a) There is no opt-out in s. 14.2; under EA-7 an opt-out must be express and contained in the arbitration agreement (the assignment memorandum's paraphrase \"opted out in writing\" is slightly imprecise; the relevant test is an express opt-out in the arbitration agreement itself). (b) The Art. 15bis.4(b) exception does not apply: the MSA was concluded on March 15, 2023, after the January 1, 2022 effective date of the 2022 Edition, and therefore after the effective date of whichever edition first introduced the procedure. (c) Section 14.3(d) affirmatively preserves emergency relief under the Rules notwithstanding the escalation procedure, so the 60-day cooling-off period is not a bar.",
"Correction to the premise that the clause lacks a court carve-out. The assignment memorandum states that the clause contains no express carve-out for interim judicial relief. In fact s. 14.3(d) expressly preserves applications \"from a court of competent jurisdiction where such relief is necessary to prevent irreparable harm\". The carve-out is helpful but is conditioned on irreparable harm. Article 15.4 independently confirms that a court application is not a waiver of the agreement to arbitrate. Greenleaf therefore has access to both routes.",
"Timing: the deletion window may already have closed for the earliest logs. Palladian estimates automated deletion 90 to 120 days after the events. For events in early June 2024, 90 days ran out at approximately the end of August 2024 and 120 days at approximately the end of September to end of October 2024. As at the date of this report, logs for June events may already have been deleted; logs for July events fall in a window closing approximately late September to late November 2024; logs for August events fall in a window closing approximately late October to late December 2024. This is a matter of days, not weeks.",
"Choice of forum for interim relief. (i) SAI emergency arbitrator: fast (appointment within 2 business days, schedule within 2 business days, decision within 15 days), decision binding on the parties (Art. 15bis.3). Under the IAA, \"arbitral tribunal\" includes an emergency arbitrator, so an emergency arbitrator's order is enforceable in Singapore with leave of the court; enforcement against Kuiper in Germany is less certain and may require a German court application. (ii) Singapore High Court under IAA s. 12A: available in support of a Singapore-seated arbitration, including in urgent cases for preservation of evidence, but under s. 12A(6) the court acts only where the tribunal or emergency arbitrator has no power or is unable to act effectively; an order against a Munich company may also face practical enforcement obstacles. (iii) German courts: Kuiper and, presumably, its servers are in Germany; German law (ZPO s. 1033, applicable to foreign-seated arbitrations by virtue of ZPO s. 1025(2)) allows a German court to order interim measures in support of an arbitration. This is likely the most directly effective route against Kuiper and should be assessed with German counsel. (iv) United States, 28 U.S.C. s. 1782: the memorandum's suggestion should not be relied upon. Section 1782 is a discovery statute, not an interim-relief mechanism, and the U.S. Supreme Court held in ZF Automotive US, Inc. v. Luxshare, Ltd., 596 U.S. 619 (2022) that private commercial arbitral tribunals (such as an SAI tribunal) are not \"foreign or international tribunals\" for s. 1782 purposes. A U.S. court would also lack obvious jurisdiction over German-hosted logs.",
"Points Kuiper may raise. (a) Whether an emergency arbitrator application may precede the Request: the SAI Rules do not require a Request to be filed first or within a set period after the application, but the SAI Secretariat should be asked to confirm its practice. (b) Data protection: logs may contain personal data subject to the EU GDPR; a preservation (not transfer) order mitigates this. (c) Confidentiality: court applications may make the dispute public, which Kuiper will characterise as a breach of the perpetual confidentiality obligation (Issue 7); applications should be filed under seal or heard in private (in Singapore, IAA ss. 22-23).",
"Interaction with the costs clause. The CHF 20,000 emergency arbitrator fee and associated legal costs may be unrecoverable given the \"each party shall bear its own costs\" language (see Issue 10), notwithstanding EA-6. The cost is modest relative to the evidentiary value of the logs."],
kuiper="Kuiper's email asks for \"reasonable advance notice\" before any Request is filed. There is no obligation to give advance notice of an emergency application beyond the escalation procedure, and doing so before a preservation undertaking is secured could increase the risk of deletion. Kuiper's assertion that the issues stem from Greenleaf's API configurations makes the server-side logs central to both sides' cases.",
recs=[
"Immediately (today) send a formal litigation hold / preservation demand to Kuiper under s. 15.3 (email and courier to Dr. Vogel at the s. 15.2 address, copied to Feldhammer Grau), identifying the log categories, systems and date ranges (June 1 - August 31, 2024 and thereafter), requiring suspension of automated deletion, and requesting a written undertaking within 48 hours. Record that any deletion after the September 12 notice will be relied upon for adverse inferences and as evidence of willful misconduct (relevant to Issue 2).",
"In parallel, prepare an emergency arbitrator application under Art. 15bis / EA-1 (description of circumstances, urgency, irreparable harm, relief sought, copy of s. 14.2, proof of CHF 20,000 fee) seeking preservation and forensic imaging of the logs by an independent expert. File if the undertaking is not received within 48 hours.",
"Instruct German counsel to prepare a parallel application to the competent Munich court (ZPO ss. 1025(2), 1033) for preservation of evidence, for filing if the emergency arbitrator route is delayed or Kuiper signals non-compliance.",
"Ask the SAI Secretariat to confirm in writing that an emergency application may be made before the Request and the escalation period has run, citing s. 14.3(d).",
"Do not pursue 28 U.S.C. s. 1782 as a source of interim relief."])

add(no="4", title="Multi-Tier Escalation Procedure as a Condition Precedent to Filing (MSA s. 14.3) and Formal Notice Requirements (s. 15.3)", sev="High",
clause="Section 14.2 is expressly \"Subject to Section 14.3\". Section 14.3: (a) a Dispute Notice describing the dispute and relief sought, delivered in accordance with s. 15.3; (b) a meeting of senior representatives (Vice President level or above) within 30 days; (c) arbitration may be commenced only if the dispute is not resolved within 60 days of delivery of the Dispute Notice. Section 15.3: notices relating to dispute resolution are effective \"only if\" sent to the s. 15.2 addresses and to General Counsel/Head of Legal by both email and international courier.",
rules="Art. 4.1 (arbitration commences when the Request is received by the Secretariat); Art. 4.2 (contents of Request); Art. 30 (waiver of right to object). The Rules contain no cooling-off or pre-arbitral negotiation requirement; this is a clause-level gap/addition rather than a conflict.",
analysis=[
"Whether the September 12, 2024 notice of breach qualifies as the Dispute Notice is not established by the materials provided. To qualify, it must (i) describe the dispute and the relief sought in reasonable detail, and (ii) have been delivered by both email and international courier to Kuiper's Head of Legal at the s. 15.2 address. We also have no record that a senior-representative meeting took place within 30 days (that is, by approximately October 12, 2024).",
"If the September 12 notice qualifies, the 60-day period expires on November 11, 2024 and the Request can be filed on or after that date (to be computed conservatively; the MSA does not adopt the Rules' Art. 3.4 counting convention). If it does not qualify, a fresh Dispute Notice must be served now and the earliest filing date moves to approximately early January 2025.",
"Singapore law treats sufficiently certain pre-arbitration escalation steps as enforceable conditions precedent (International Research Corp PLC v. Lufthansa Systems Asia Pacific Pte Ltd [2013] SGCA 55). Premature filing exposes Greenleaf to a jurisdictional or admissibility objection, a stay, or wasted costs (which, given Issue 10, would be unrecoverable). Whether non-compliance goes to jurisdiction or admissibility is contested in Singapore jurisprudence (cf. BBA v. BAZ [2020] SGCA 53, on the tribunal/claim distinction) and should be confirmed with Singapore counsel.",
"Notice-address discrepancies. Kuiper's October 28 email was sent from k.vogel@kuiper-data.de and addressed to m.yuen@greenleafbio.com. Section 15.2 specifies k.vogel@kuiperdata.de and myuen@greenleafbio.com. We have seen no notice of change of address under s. 15.3 (final paragraph). Because s. 15.3 makes dispute-resolution notices effective \"only if\" properly delivered, Greenleaf should serve at the contractual addresses and, protectively, at the address actually in use, plus courier. Kuiper has also asked that Dr. Feldhammer and Dr. Grau be copied; s. 15.2 lists Feldhammer Grau's general address (info@feldhammer-grau.de, Maximilianstrasse 34) as a non-notice copy. Copy all of them.",
"Language of notices. Section 15.4 requires all Notices to be in English, which is consistent with Greenleaf's position on Issue 6."],
kuiper="Kuiper's request for \"reasonable advance notice\" and to \"explore whether a more efficient resolution is possible\" is an opening that Greenleaf can use to convene the s. 14.3(b) senior-representative meeting promptly, thereby curing any defect in the escalation record while preserving the filing timetable.",
recs=[
"Pull the September 12, 2024 notice and proof of delivery (email and courier receipts). Confirm whether it meets s. 14.3(a) and s. 15.3.",
"Regardless of the answer, serve a short protective Dispute Notice now (English; email and courier; to both Kuiper email domains, the s. 15.2 postal address, Dr. Vogel, and copied to Feldhammer Grau) that expressly invokes s. 14.3 and states the relief sought, and propose dates for a VP-level meeting by videoconference within the next 10 days.",
"Document the meeting (or Kuiper's refusal) so that the condition precedent is demonstrably satisfied when the Request is filed.",
"Do not file the Request before the 60-day period has expired on a conservative calculation. Emergency relief (Issue 3) is not subject to this constraint (s. 14.3(d))."])

add(no="5", title="15-Day Window for Agreement on the Sole Arbitrator", sev="High",
clause="\"The arbitration shall be conducted by a sole arbitrator mutually agreed upon by the parties within 15 calendar days of the filing of the Request for Arbitration.\" (MSA s. 14.2). The clause contains no fallback if agreement is not reached.",
rules="Art. 6.4 (parties shall endeavour to agree within 30 calendar days of the filing of the Request; failing agreement \"within that period\", the SAI Court appoints); Art. 4.1 (filing = receipt by Secretariat); Art. 4.3 (Secretariat transmits the Request to the Respondent only upon receipt of the filing fee); Art. 3.4 (time periods run from the day after receipt); Art. 4.2(f) (Request must name any proposed sole arbitrator or propose a method of appointment); Art. 8.1 (SAI Court confirmation and declaration of independence required for constitution); Art. 1.4 (party agreement prevails).",
analysis=[
"Deviation. The clause halves the Rules' 30-day period. Article 6.4 is not designated mandatory and is expressed as a default \"endeavour\" provision; under Art. 1.4 the parties' 15-day period should prevail. The 15-day period is not contrary to Singapore law (Model Law Art. 11(2) leaves the appointment procedure to the parties).",
"Gap. The clause does not say what happens on day 16. Read with the Rules, the SAI Court's default appointment power under Art. 6.4 fills the gap; the arbitration agreement is therefore not pathological. But Art. 6.4 refers to failure to agree \"within that period\", meaning the 30-day period, creating an argument (which Kuiper has previewed) that the SAI Court may not act until day 30. The better view is that the contractual 15-day period substitutes for the Rules' 30-day period, so that the SAI Court's power arises on day 16.",
"Practical compression. The 15 days run from filing (receipt by the Secretariat, Art. 4.1), yet Kuiper receives the Request only when the Secretariat transmits it after the filing fee is received (Art. 4.3), and Rules periods run from the day after receipt (Art. 3.4). Kuiper may in practice have materially fewer than 15 days, which strengthens a fairness argument for flexibility and undermines any attempt by Greenleaf to insist rigidly on the deadline.",
"Merit of Kuiper's position. Kuiper's statement that it \"will not consider itself bound by the 15-day contractual deadline\" is legally weak: it agreed to the deadline, and its own counsel drafted the clause. Article 1.4 gives the parties' agreement priority. However, a dispute about the appointment timetable is itself a potential ground of later challenge under Model Law Art. 34(2)(a)(iv) (composition of the tribunal not in accordance with the agreement) whichever way the SAI Court rules. Either side that proceeds without objection risks waiver under Art. 30, so Greenleaf must object promptly to Kuiper's stated position.",
"Strategic assessment. A fast appointment helps Greenleaf only if the resulting tribunal is uncontroversial. Greenleaf's real interests are (a) an early constitution for interim relief (largely addressed by the emergency arbitrator, Issue 3) and (b) an unimpeachable appointment. Kuiper's request for more time is a bargaining chip that can be traded for relief on the 90-day award deadline (Issue 1)."],
kuiper="Kuiper asserts that the 15-day window is impracticable and inconsistent with Art. 6, that it will rely on 30 days, and that it will object to any SAI Court appointment before day 30. Assessment: inconsistent with Art. 1.4 and with the clause Kuiper itself proposed; the objection must nonetheless be answered in writing to avoid any later waiver argument (Art. 30).",
recs=[
"Respond in writing to the October 28 email rejecting Kuiper's position, reserving Greenleaf's rights under s. 14.2 and Art. 1.4, while offering a negotiated package (Part F): e.g., a written agreement extending the appointment window to 30 days (or 21 days) in exchange for replacing the 90-day award deadline.",

add(no="6", title="Dual Language (English and German) with Submissions in Either Language", sev="High",
clause="\"The language of the arbitration shall be English and German, with all submissions accepted in either language.\" (MSA s. 14.2). Section 15.4: all Notices in English; supporting documents in another language to be accompanied by an English translation.",
rules="Art. 12.1 (language(s) as agreed); Art. 12.2 (where more than one language is designated, the tribunal determines procedures, including (a) language of written submissions, (b) hearings, (c) the award, and (d) translation/interpretation and cost); Art. 12.4 (tribunal may order translations of documents in a language other than the language(s) of the arbitration); Art. 4.2(e) / 5.1(e) (observations on language in Request and Answer).",
analysis=[
"Deviation and gap. Designating two languages is permitted (Art. 12.1). The clause fixes one element (submissions may be in either language), which binds the tribunal and narrows its Art. 12.2(a) discretion. The clause is silent on hearings, witness evidence, the language of the award, translation and interpretation, and who bears their cost. Those matters fall to the tribunal under Art. 12.2(b)-(d). Because both English and German are languages of the arbitration, Art. 12.4 does not by itself entitle Greenleaf to translations of Kuiper's German submissions or documents: they are not in a language \"other than the language(s) of the arbitration\".",
"Assessment of Kuiper's positions. (a) German as co-equal language: correct as far as it goes; the clause gives both languages equal status. (b) Kuiper's right to file all of its submissions in German: supported by the literal text (\"all submissions accepted in either language\"). (c) Award in German: not supported. The clause is silent on the language of the award, and Art. 12.2(c) gives the tribunal the decision. Kuiper's assertion that the MSA was \"negotiated in significant part in German\" is unverified and is contradicted by the record we have: the MSA is in English, Greenleaf was represented by its U.S. General Counsel, the governing law is New York law, the seat is Singapore (an English-language jurisdiction whose courts will hear any set-aside application in English), and s. 15.4 requires all contractual Notices to be in English. These factors strongly support an English award (or at least an English authoritative version).",
"Enforceability and cost. If the award is in German, enforcement in the U.S. or Singapore would require a certified translation (New York Convention Art. IV(2)); any set-aside proceeding in Singapore would be in English. The clause, combined with the each-party-bears-own-costs provision (Issue 10), means Greenleaf would likely bear the cost of translating Kuiper's German submissions, exhibits and witness evidence for its own team and witnesses, with no recovery. The bilingual requirement also materially narrows the pool of suitable arbitrators (who must also satisfy the expertise and availability constraints in Issues 1 and 5) and lengthens every phase of a proceeding already constrained by the 90-day deadline.",
"Strategic implications. Kuiper's stated intention to file everything in German is a cost and time lever against Greenleaf. Greenleaf cannot prevent German submissions, but it can seek directions under Art. 12.2(d) that (i) hearings be conducted in English with simultaneous interpretation, (ii) the award be rendered in English, (iii) translations of German submissions and key exhibits into English be provided by the filing party (or costs be shared), and (iv) English be the language of the tribunal's procedural orders."],
kuiper="Kuiper expects all substantive submissions, witness statements and expert reports in German and an award in German. Assessment: entitled to file in German; no entitlement to a German award, which is for the tribunal under Art. 12.2(c); its factual premise regarding German negotiation is unproven and contrary to the documentary record.",
recs=[
"File the Request and all Greenleaf materials in English. In the Request (Art. 4.2(e)), state Greenleaf's position that the award and procedural orders should be in English and that the party submitting non-English material should provide English translations.",
"Respond to the October 28 email: acknowledge the clause permits submissions in either language; reject the proposition that the award must be in German; reserve the issue for the tribunal under Art. 12.2.",
"Gather evidence on the negotiating history (drafts, correspondence, meeting languages) to rebut the \"negotiated in German\" assertion.",
"Prefer arbitrator candidates with working German so that the tribunal can read German materials without delay, while insisting on English as the language of the award.",

add(no="7", title="Perpetual Confidentiality Without Exceptions", sev="High",
clause="\"All arbitration proceedings, including the existence of the arbitration and any awards, shall remain strictly confidential in perpetuity.\" (MSA s. 14.2)",
rules="Art. 20.1 (proceedings, existence, submissions, evidence, materials, awards and orders confidential); Art. 20.2 (permitted disclosures: (a) as required by law, regulation or legal process including securities and regulatory filings; (b) to protect or pursue a legal right before a court or regulator; (c) enforcement or challenge of an award; (d) with written consent; (e) to professional advisors bound by professional duties of confidentiality); Art. 20.3 (Rules obligation survives for five years after the final award, without prejudice to confidentiality obligations under the underlying agreement or applicable law); Art. 20.4 (protective orders); Art. 16.4 (hearings private).",
analysis=[
"Duration conflict. The clause is perpetual; Art. 20.3 ends the Rules-based obligation five years after the final award. Article 20.3 expressly preserves longer contractual obligations, so the perpetual duty prevails. This is a permitted extension, not a conflict with a mandatory Rule.",
"Absence of exceptions (key gap). The clause contains none of the Art. 20.2 exceptions. A literal reading would bar disclosure even where required by law, for enforcement, to regulators, or to advisors. Arguments that the exceptions survive: (a) the clause incorporates the Rules, and the Art. 20.2 exceptions are part of the regime the parties adopted; (b) Art. 20.3 confirms the contractual obligation operates alongside the Rules; (c) a contractual confidentiality obligation cannot override mandatory legal disclosure obligations (public policy under both New York and Singapore law); (d) Singapore law recognises an implied duty of confidentiality in arbitration subject to exceptions such as disclosure reasonably necessary to protect a party's legitimate interests or required by law (see, e.g., AAY v. AAZ [2009] SGHC 142). The counter-argument is that by specifying a stricter regime the parties intended to exclude the Rules' exceptions. The point should be resolved by agreement or tribunal order rather than left to dispute.",
"Scope. The clause covers \"arbitration proceedings, including the existence of the arbitration and any awards\". It does not, on its terms, extend to (i) the underlying facts (the data corruption and outages); (ii) the existence of a commercial dispute before arbitration is commenced; (iii) pre-arbitral correspondence such as the September 12 notice and the October 3 response; or (iv) Greenleaf's own business records and forensic findings. Kuiper's assertion that the obligation already extends to \"all information relating to the dispute\" overstates the clause.",
"Regulatory and disclosure exposure for Greenleaf. Greenleaf's damages include FDA regulatory re-submissions arising from corruption of three clinical trial databases; Greenleaf will necessarily communicate with the FDA (and possibly trial sponsors, CROs, investigators and IRBs) about data integrity. If Greenleaf is publicly traded (described as \"mid-cap\"; to be confirmed), it may have SEC disclosure obligations regarding material legal proceedings and risks. It may also need to disclose to auditors, insurers and lenders. Kuiper's position that Greenleaf may not disclose \"to any third party\", read as including regulators, is untenable as a matter of law and public policy; Art. 20.2(a) and (b) expressly contemplate regulatory disclosures.",
"Forensic experts and service providers. Art. 20.2(e) permits disclosure to professional advisors \"bound by professional duties of confidentiality\". A forensic technology firm such as Palladian may not be bound by professional (as opposed to contractual) duties. Greenleaf should ensure Palladian and any other consultants are under written confidentiality undertakings and are engaged through counsel to support privilege.",
"Court applications. Emergency and enforcement applications (Issue 3) will disclose the existence of the arbitration. Seek sealing / private hearings (IAA ss. 22-23 in Singapore; equivalent measures elsewhere) and rely on Art. 20.2(b)-(c)."],
kuiper="Kuiper asserts that the perpetual obligation covers the existence of the dispute, all correspondence, its October 3 response, and all future filings, and that Greenleaf, its advisors, consultants and forensic experts may not disclose anything to any third party; it reserves rights for breach. Assessment: overbroad. The clause covers the arbitration proceedings, their existence and awards, not the pre-arbitral dispute or underlying facts; it cannot lawfully prevent legally required disclosures to regulators; and advisor/expert disclosure for the purpose of the arbitration is inherent in the right to arbitrate and is expressly permitted by Art. 20.2(e).",
recs=[
"Respond to the October 28 email rejecting Kuiper's interpretation, confirming Greenleaf will comply with s. 14.2 as properly construed, and stating that Greenleaf will make disclosures required by law or regulation (including to the FDA and, if applicable, the SEC) and to its professional advisors and experts under confidentiality undertakings.",
"Propose a written confidentiality protocol (for inclusion in Terms of Reference or a procedural order under Art. 20.4) that expressly incorporates the Art. 20.2 exceptions on a perpetual basis.",
"Confirm with regulatory counsel what FDA and securities disclosures are required and their timing; prepare those disclosures to describe facts rather than arbitral filings where possible.",
"Put written NDAs in place with Palladian and any other non-lawyer advisors; route engagements through Thorncastle & Whitmore."])

add(no="8", title="Discovery Limited to Document Production Only", sev="High",
clause="\"Discovery shall be limited to document production only ...\" (MSA s. 14.2)",
rules="Art. 14.3 and 18.2 (tribunal may order production of documents, exhibits or other evidence and take evidence by witness testimony, expert evidence, site inspections and any other means); Art. 14.4 and 17.3 (tribunal-appointed experts); Art. 14.5 and 17.1, 17.4 (party witness statements and expert reports); Art. 17.2 (tribunal may order a person, including a party's officer or employee, to appear); Art. 13.3(c) (case management of document production, witnesses and experts); Art. 15.1(a) (interim preservation orders).",
analysis=[
"Deviation. The Rules confer broad evidentiary powers on the tribunal. The clause restricts \"discovery\" to document production. Depositions, interrogatories and requests for admission are not features of the Rules or of international arbitration practice in any event, so excluding them changes little.",
"Ambiguity that matters. \"Discovery\" is a U.S. term without a defined meaning in the Rules. Kuiper may argue it excludes (i) inspection of Kuiper's servers, systems and environments (Art. 18.2 site inspection); (ii) forensic imaging or access to native data and logs; (iii) tribunal orders requiring Kuiper personnel to attend (Art. 17.2); and (iv) tribunal-appointed experts with access to Kuiper's systems (Art. 14.4 / 17.3). Greenleaf's position should be that (a) \"discovery\" refers only to compelled disclosure from the opposing party, not to the presentation of evidence (witness statements and expert reports under Arts. 14.5 and 17 remain fully available); (b) \"documents\" include electronically stored information such as server logs, audit trails and configuration records in native format; and (c) interim preservation orders under Art. 15.1(a) and the emergency arbitrator procedure are not \"discovery\" at all.",
"Strategic implications. The key evidence on causation (Kuiper server logs, incident tickets, change records, root-cause analyses) is in Kuiper's control, and Greenleaf bears the burden of proof (Art. 14.2). A narrow reading of the limitation, if combined with log deletion, would severely prejudice Greenleaf. The limitation is enforceable as a party agreement (Art. 1.4), but must be applied consistently with each party's right to a reasonable opportunity to present its case (Art. 18.1; Model Law Art. 18), which supports a broad reading of \"document production\" in respect of electronic records.",
"Interaction with the 90-day deadline. Even document production on electronic data is unlikely to be completed within the 90-day window (Issue 1)."],
kuiper=None,
recs=[
"In the Request and at the case management conference (Art. 13.3(c)), seek directions that \"documents\" include ESI and native-format logs and metadata, and that inspection of systems by a tribunal-appointed or jointly appointed neutral forensic expert is within the tribunal's power.",
"Seek preservation and forensic imaging through the emergency arbitrator now (Issue 3) so that the evidence exists by the time document production takes place.",
"Prepare targeted, Redfern-style document requests focused on log data, incident reports and root-cause analyses for June-August 2024.",
"Ask the tribunal to confirm that adverse inferences may be drawn from non-production or destruction of logs after the September 12 notice."])

add(no="9", title="Sole Arbitrator Despite Amount in Controversy Above the CHF 5 Million Three-Member Default", sev="Moderate",
clause="\"The arbitration shall be conducted by a sole arbitrator ...\" (MSA s. 14.2)",
rules="Art. 6.2 (agreement on number given effect, subject to Art. 6.5); Art. 6.3 (CHF 5,000,000 threshold for a three-member default applies only \"where the parties have not agreed\"); Art. 6.5 (SAI Court may, in exceptional circumstances and on a reasoned request of a party, determine a different number); Art. 5.3 (counterclaims treated as separate claims for amount-in-controversy purposes, including Art. 6 and Appendix I); Appendix I (fees).",
analysis=[
"No conflict with the default rule. The memorandum's concern requires a correction of emphasis: the CHF 5 million threshold in Art. 6.3(a) is a default that applies only where the parties have not agreed on the number. Here they have agreed on a sole arbitrator, and Art. 6.2 directs that the agreement be given effect. The amount in controversy does not, by itself, entitle the SAI Court to override the clause.",
"Residual risk: Article 6.5. The SAI Court may depart from the agreed number \"in exceptional circumstances and upon the reasoned request of a party\". Kuiper (or Greenleaf) could invoke it, pointing to the amount in dispute (Greenleaf's claim of $11.9 million is approximately CHF 10.6 million on the exchange rate in the memorandum; with the counterclaim, $13.3 million is approximately CHF 11.9 million), technical complexity, and the dual-language regime. Value alone is unlikely to be \"exceptional\" for a CHF 10-12 million dispute, so the risk of an override is moderate-to-low. Under Art. 5.3 the counterclaim is treated as a separate claim; on either an aggregated or separate measure, Greenleaf's claim alone exceeds CHF 5 million.",
"Seat-law risk if the number is changed. If the SAI Court imposed three arbitrators over a party's objection, the opposing party could argue that the composition of the tribunal was not in accordance with the agreement of the parties (Model Law Art. 34(2)(a)(iv); New York Convention Art. V(1)(d)). The counter-argument is that the parties agreed to the Rules, including Art. 6.5. The risk is real but limited.",
"Strategic assessment for Greenleaf. A sole arbitrator is consistent with Greenleaf's interest in speed and cost (indicative sole-arbitrator fees of CHF 50,000-200,000 versus CHF 120,000-500,000 for a three-member tribunal in the CHF 5-20 million band, Appendix I Part III), particularly given that Greenleaf will bear its own costs (Issue 10). The downside is single-decision-maker risk on difficult construction questions (Issue 2) and heavy dependence on the quality of the appointee. Kuiper has not yet sought a three-member tribunal; it may do so if it perceives tactical advantage, for example to escape the 90-day deadline.",
"Fees (Appendix I). In the CHF 5,000,001-20,000,000 band: filing fee CHF 5,000 (payable by Greenleaf on filing, non-refundable); SAI administrative charges CHF 25,000-60,000; sole arbitrator fees indicatively CHF 50,000-200,000; emergency arbitrator fee CHF 20,000. If Art. 5.3 is applied so that the counterclaim is assessed separately, the counterclaim (approximately CHF 1.25 million) would fall in a lower band."],
kuiper="Not addressed in Kuiper's email.",
recs=[
"Do not challenge the sole-arbitrator designation. State in the Request that the parties have agreed a sole arbitrator under Art. 6.2.",
"If Kuiper makes an Art. 6.5 application, oppose it as not \"exceptional\", but consider whether a three-member tribunal could be traded for an agreed, realistic award timetable.",
"Confirm the CHF/USD rate at filing for Appendix I purposes and quantify the claim in a manner that does not inadvertently push into a higher fee band without need."])

add(no="10", title="Each Party Bears Its Own Costs Regardless of Outcome", sev="Moderate",
clause="\"... each party shall bear its own costs regardless of the outcome.\" (MSA s. 14.2)",
rules="Art. 25.4 (award shall fix costs and decide allocation); Art. 26.1 (costs of arbitration include arbitrator fees and expenses, SAI administrative charges, tribunal-expert fees, and reasonable legal costs); Art. 26.3 (tribunal allocates costs; party agreements on allocation given effect unless \"manifestly unreasonable\"); Art. 26.4-26.5 and 27 (advances in equal shares; a party may pay the defaulting party's share); Art. 34.1(e) (costs as relief); EA-6 (emergency arbitrator may allocate EA costs).",
analysis=[
"Deviation. The clause displaces the tribunal's default discretion to allocate costs by reference to outcome and conduct (Art. 26.3). Under Art. 26.3 the agreement will be given effect unless the tribunal considers it \"manifestly unreasonable in the circumstances of the case\", a significant safety valve that the clause does not (and cannot) exclude.",
"Ambiguity: which costs? \"Its own costs\" most naturally refers to each party's own legal and expert costs (Art. 26.1(d)). It is unclear whether it also fixes the shared costs of the arbitration (arbitrator fees, SAI charges, tribunal-appointed expert fees under Art. 26.1(a)-(c)), which are not any one party's \"own\" costs. Greenleaf should argue that the clause covers only party-incurred costs, leaving the tribunal free to allocate the shared costs of the arbitration, and also the cost of the emergency arbitrator proceeding under EA-6.",
"Strategic impact on Greenleaf. As the claimant with what it believes to be the stronger case, Greenleaf loses the cost-shifting leverage that normally accompanies a meritorious claim; net recovery will be reduced by its full legal, forensic, translation and interpretation spend. If Kuiper defaults on its share of the advance (Art. 26.5), Greenleaf may have to fund it to keep the case alive with uncertain recovery. Costs of satellite disputes (escalation compliance, appointment timetable, language, confidentiality) are also borne by Greenleaf. The clause is consistent with the American Rule under New York law and is likely enforceable.",
"Manifest unreasonableness. Conduct such as spoliation of server logs, obstructive procedural tactics, or bad-faith counterclaims could support an Art. 26.3 argument that applying the clause would be manifestly unreasonable."],
kuiper=None,
recs=[
"Build the costs budget on the assumption that legal and expert costs are unrecoverable; factor this into settlement valuation.",
"Plead that the clause covers only party-incurred costs and request allocation of arbitration costs (Art. 26.1(a)-(c)) and emergency arbitrator costs (EA-6) by outcome.",
"Keep a record of Kuiper's procedural conduct to support an Art. 26.3 \"manifestly unreasonable\" argument if warranted.",
"Consider including cost allocation in the pre-filing procedural package (Part F)."])

add(no="11", title="Temporal Lock to the Rules \"in Effect at the Time of the Signing\" (2022 Edition)", sev="Moderate",
clause="\"... in accordance with the SAI Arbitration Rules in effect at the time of the signing of this Agreement.\" (MSA s. 14.2; signed March 15, 2023)",
rules="Preamble (where a specific edition is referenced, SAI administers under that edition \"subject to any modifications the SAI Court deems necessary for proper administration\"); Art. 35.1 (2022 Rules apply to arbitrations filed on or after January 1, 2022); Art. 35.3 (where a specific prior edition is referenced, SAI administers under it \"to the extent practicable\" and may apply procedural or administrative provisions of the current edition provided this does not prejudice either party); Art. 2.10.",
analysis=[
"Identification of the edition. The 2022 Edition took effect on January 1, 2022 and, on the materials provided, was in effect on March 15, 2023. It is therefore the edition locked in by the clause. We have not been provided with the 2024 Edition (stated in the memorandum to be effective July 1, 2024) and cannot assess its changes; nor can we exclude interim amendments between January 2022 and March 2023. Both should be confirmed with the SAI Secretariat.",
"Administrative risk. Once the 2024 Edition is in force, the reference to the 2022 Edition is to a superseded edition. The Preamble and Art. 35.3 (assuming the 2024 Edition contains an equivalent transitional provision) allow the SAI to apply current procedural or administrative provisions where it considers this necessary and non-prejudicial. This introduces uncertainty about, for example, fee scales, emergency arbitrator mechanics, time limits and expedited procedures. If the 2024 Edition contains provisions favourable to Greenleaf (for example, expedited procedures or clearer emergency arbitrator rules), Greenleaf may wish to agree with Kuiper to apply them; if it contains unfavourable provisions, Greenleaf should insist on the 2022 Edition.",
"Enforceability. Application of an edition other than the one agreed, if prejudicial, could be raised under Model Law Art. 34(2)(a)(iv). The risk is low if the SAI confines itself to administrative matters."],
kuiper="Kuiper's email refers to the \"SAI Rules (2022 Edition)\" (citing Art. 12 and Art. 6), so both parties appear to accept that the 2022 Edition governs.",
recs=[
"Obtain the 2024 Edition and any 2022-2023 amendments; prepare a short comparison focused on Arts. 6, 12, 15bis/Appendix II, 20, 24, 26 and Appendix I.",

"Decide, after the comparison, whether to propose to Kuiper the application of any 2024 provisions."])

add(no="12", title="Waiver of \"Any Right to Appeal the Award on Any Grounds\"", sev="Low",
clause="\"The parties waive any right to appeal the award on any grounds.\" (MSA s. 14.2)",
rules="Art. 29.1 (award binding; undertaking to carry out without delay); Art. 29.2 (waiver of recourse insofar as validly waivable under applicable law); Art. 29.3 (non-waivable set-aside rights at the seat unaffected); Art. 28 (correction, interpretation, additional award within 30 days).",
analysis=[
"Scope correction. The assignment memorandum describes this as a waiver \"including any right to set aside the award\". The clause text does not say that: it waives a right to \"appeal\". An appeal (review on the merits) is conceptually distinct from an application to set aside an award on limited grounds.",
"Consistency with the Rules and seat law. The waiver mirrors Art. 29.2. Under the IAA there is in any event no appeal on questions of law (that mechanism exists only in the domestic Arbitration Act 2001). The setting-aside grounds under Model Law Art. 34 and IAA s. 24 (fraud, corruption, breach of natural justice) are generally regarded in Singapore as non-excludable by party agreement; Art. 29.3 confirms the Rules do not purport to exclude them. Resistance to recognition and enforcement under New York Convention Art. V is likewise unaffected. To the extent the waiver were read as purporting to exclude set-aside, it would be ineffective, but it would not invalidate the arbitration agreement.",
"Strategic implications. The waiver is mutual. It cuts against Greenleaf if the tribunal misapplies New York law on the damages exclusion (Issue 2), since a merits error is not a set-aside ground. Conversely, the set-aside routes that remain (procedure not in accordance with the agreement; excess of mandate) are precisely those engaged by Issues 1, 2, 4 and 5, which is why those issues should be resolved by agreement before or early in the proceedings. Because the seat is Singapore, U.S. courts have only secondary (enforcement) jurisdiction and could not vacate the award under the FAA.",
"Correction requests under Art. 28 are unaffected and should be calendared (30 days from receipt of the award)."],
kuiper=None,
recs=[
"No pre-filing action required on the waiver itself. Ensure that any objections that could ground a set-aside (Issues 1, 4, 5) are raised promptly to avoid waiver under Art. 30 and Model Law Art. 4.",
"Correct the characterisation in client-facing materials: the waiver does not extend to set-aside."])

add(no="13", title="Bifurcated Legal Regime: New York Governing Law and Singapore Seat; Law of the Arbitration Agreement", sev="Low",
clause="MSA s. 14.1 (New York law governs the Agreement and all claims arising out of or relating to it; CISG excluded; procedural law of any arbitration determined by the seat); s. 14.2 (seat Singapore). No express law governing the arbitration agreement.",
rules="Art. 10.1, 10.3, 10.4 (seat as agreed; hearings may be elsewhere; award deemed made at seat); Art. 11.1 and 23.1 (substantive law as designated; designation refers to substantive law, not conflict rules); Art. 33 (tribunal to ensure enforceability); Art. 1.2 and 1.4(b) (party modifications subject to the law of the seat).",
analysis=[
"Allocation. Substance (breach, damages, construction of ss. 12 and 14.2, enforceability of exclusions and the cap) is governed by New York law (s. 14.1; Art. 23.1). Procedure, the tribunal's mandate, interim measures in support, and set-aside are governed by Singapore law (IAA and Model Law) (s. 14.1(b); Art. 10.4).",
"Gap. The clause does not specify the law governing the arbitration agreement itself. Under Singapore choice-of-law principles, an express choice of law for the main contract is a strong indicator of the law governing an arbitration agreement contained within it (BCY v. BCZ [2016] SGHC 249; see also Anupam Mittal v. Westbridge Ventures II Investment Holdings [2023] SGCA 1 on arbitrability, which considers both the law of the arbitration agreement and the law of the seat). New York law is therefore likely to govern questions such as the construction of the scope of the arbitrator's authority (e.g., the damages exclusion), while Singapore law governs whether the tribunal stayed within that authority for set-aside purposes. The breadth of s. 14.1 (\"all claims ... that may be based upon, arise out of, or relate to this Agreement\") supports this.",
"Where the regimes may conflict. (a) Damages exclusion: enforceability under New York law (including the Kalisch-Jarcho public-policy limit) versus excess-of-mandate review at the seat (Issue 2). (b) Award deadline: an issue of seat procedure, but the agreed deadline is construed as a contractual term (Issue 1). (c) Confidentiality: New York contract law governs the express obligation; Singapore law supplies the implied duty and its exceptions and governs court confidentiality (Issue 7). (d) Escalation: Singapore law on conditions precedent may apply to admissibility/jurisdiction (Issue 4). (e) Jury waiver (s. 14.5) is relevant only to any U.S. court proceeding and has no effect on the arbitration.",
"Related observation (s. 14.4 continued performance). Section 14.4 requires both parties to continue performing pending resolution. Greenleaf's withholding of $1.4 million of invoices is the basis of Kuiper's counterclaim; Kuiper may also allege breach of s. 14.4. Greenleaf should be prepared to justify withholding (e.g., set-off, non-performance, or an express contractual right in Schedule B or Section 7) under New York law."],
kuiper=None,

"Engage Singapore counsel (procedure, s. 12A interim relief, set-aside risk) and German counsel (interim relief in Munich, enforcement against Kuiper) now; New York counsel (this firm) to lead on substance.",
"Analyse Greenleaf's contractual basis for withholding the $1.4 million and its exposure under s. 14.4."])
